title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Confirm the Syndrome, Then Judge Severity
bottomLine: Do not prescribe antibiotics for every cough. In ambulatory care, pneumonia becomes more likely when compatible lower-respiratory symptoms occur with abnormal vital signs or focal chest findings; confirm with chest radiography when pneumonia is suspected and use severity, oxygenation, comorbidity and social reliability to choose outpatient versus acute-care management.
recognize: Fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, hypoxemia and focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds can support pneumonia.
Older adults may present with weakness, delirium or functional decline rather than prominent fever and cough.
Normal vital signs plus a normal respiratory examination make pneumonia substantially less likely in otherwise stable ambulatory patients.
differentiate: Acute bronchitis is usually viral and does not require antibiotics.
Heart failure, pulmonary embolism, COPD or asthma exacerbation and viral infection can mimic pneumonia.
A chest radiograph is not needed for every uncomplicated URI, but suspected pneumonia should not be diagnosed solely from sputum colour.
assessment: Assess respiratory rate, oxygenation, blood pressure, mental status, hydration, comorbidity, immune status, pregnancy and ability to take oral therapy.
Ask recent antibiotics, aspiration risk, travel or outbreak exposure and prior resistant organisms when these could alter treatment.
workup: Obtain chest radiography when clinical findings make pneumonia plausible and imaging is available; additional cultures and laboratory tests are reserved for severe, complicated or treatment-failure presentations.
Use a validated severity tool only as an adjunct to clinical judgment, especially in frailty, pregnancy or major comorbidity.
management: Treat confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial CAP with a locally recommended regimen matched to comorbidity and resistance risk.

Choosing Wisely Canada's ambulatory Cold Standard recommends short-course therapy for uncomplicated pneumonia when the patient is clinically stable; hospitalized or unstable patients require a different pathway.
Escalate for significant hypoxemia, hypotension, confusion, respiratory distress, inability to hydrate or concern for sepsis.
medicationSafety: Check allergy history, renal and hepatic function, pregnancy, QT-prolonging interactions and recent antibiotic exposure.
Do not broaden therapy simply because sputum is green or yellow.
counselling: Explain expected improvement and specific return precautions for worsening dyspnea, persistent fever, confusion, dehydration or chest pain.
followUp: Reassess if symptoms fail to improve as expected; do not routinely order follow-up chest imaging in every clinically recovered low-risk patient unless another indication exists.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for acute bronchitis because sputum is coloured, or ruling out pneumonia without checking vital signs and oxygenation.
oneLinePearl: Pneumonia is a respiratory syndrome plus objective concern—not a sputum-colour diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Cold Standard
Choosing Wisely Canada Using Antibiotics Wisely in Primary Care

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Screen, Confirm, Treat the Risk
bottomLine: Snoring alone is not OSA and a screening questionnaire does not make the diagnosis. Use symptoms and risk factors to estimate pre-test probability, confirm suspected OSA with an appropriate sleep study, then treat according to severity, symptoms, comorbidity, patient preference and safety risks such as drowsy driving.
recognize: Loud habitual snoring, witnessed apneas, gasping or choking, nonrestorative sleep and excessive daytime sleepiness raise suspicion.
Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, obesity, craniofacial anatomy and cardiometabolic disease increase pre-test probability, but OSA can occur without obesity.
Drowsy driving or safety-sensitive work makes untreated sleepiness an immediate safety issue.
differentiate: Insomnia, insufficient sleep, restless legs, depression, medications, alcohol, hypothyroidism and central sleep apnea can cause fatigue or sleepiness.
STOP-Bang and similar tools stratify risk but do not replace diagnostic sleep testing.
assessment: Ask snoring, witnessed events, daytime sleepiness, sleep duration, insomnia, alcohol or sedatives, nasal obstruction, cardiovascular disease and driving or occupational safety.
Assess BP, airway or craniofacial factors and relevant cardiometabolic comorbidity.
workup: Use home sleep apnea testing for appropriately selected uncomplicated adults with a high pre-test probability when the local pathway supports it; use laboratory polysomnography when another sleep disorder, significant comorbidity or a nondiagnostic home test makes it necessary.
Do not use nocturnal oximetry alone as a universal diagnostic substitute.
management: Positive airway pressure is a highly effective treatment for many patients with clinically important OSA; oral appliance therapy, positional strategies, weight management and selected surgical approaches may be appropriate depending on phenotype and preference.
Address alcohol, sedatives and sleep deprivation when they worsen disease or safety risk.
medicationSafety: Sedative-hypnotics, opioids and alcohol can worsen sleep-disordered breathing or daytime impairment in susceptible patients.
Avoid prescribing wake-promoting medication as a substitute for treating inadequately managed OSA or insufficient sleep.
redFlags: Severe daytime sleepiness with driving or workplace risk
Failure or intolerance of therapy with persistent severe symptoms
counselling: Discuss adherence barriers to PAP without framing nonuse as patient failure; mask fit, pressure comfort and access often determine success.
Advise patients not to drive when dangerously sleepy and follow jurisdictional fitness-to-drive rules.
followUp: Review symptom response, PAP or device data when available, adherence, BP and residual sleepiness; reconsider the diagnosis if symptoms persist despite effective therapy.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from a high STOP-Bang score without a sleep study or treating fatigue with stimulants before addressing untreated OSA.
oneLinePearl: Questionnaires find risk; sleep testing confirms OSA.
sourceBasis: Primary Care Alberta Provincial Adult OSA Clinical Pathway 2025
BC Guideline: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Assessment and Management in Adults

title: Cirrhosis: Recognize Decompensation
bottomLine: A patient with cirrhosis who develops new ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, jaundice with systemic decline, kidney injury or infection has decompensated disease and needs rapid cause-finding and escalation. Do not use an elevated ammonia level by itself to diagnose or grade hepatic encephalopathy.
recognize: Decompensation commonly presents with ascites, edema, GI bleeding, confusion or sleep-wake reversal, jaundice, infection or renal dysfunction.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis can present subtly with worsening ascites, encephalopathy, renal dysfunction or systemic decline rather than dramatic abdominal pain.
Cirrhosis-associated coagulation tests do not reflect a simple auto-anticoagulated state.
differentiate: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis after considering other causes of altered mental status such as infection, medication toxicity, bleeding, electrolyte disturbance, hypoglycemia and intracranial disease.
A high ammonia level alone does not establish the diagnosis or severity of encephalopathy.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, mental status, bleeding, ascites, infection symptoms, alcohol or substance use, medications, bowel pattern, volume status and renal function.
Look for precipitants of encephalopathy such as GI bleed, constipation, infection, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and sedating medications.
workup: New or worsening clinically significant ascites with decompensation or hospital presentation often requires diagnostic paracentesis through an acute-care pathway.
Use CBC, renal and hepatic tests, electrolytes, coagulation studies and infection workup according to presentation; do not order serial ammonia levels to track clinical response.
management: GI bleeding, suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, significant encephalopathy, AKI or hemodynamic instability requires hospital-level care.
Treat the precipitating cause and use evidence-based encephalopathy, ascites and portal-hypertension therapies through hepatology or local pathways.
Refer appropriate decompensated patients for hepatology and transplant assessment rather than repeatedly treating complications in isolation.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary NSAIDs and review sedatives, opioids, benzodiazepines and nephrotoxic drugs carefully in cirrhosis.
Do not routinely correct abnormal INR or platelet counts with plasma or platelets before low-risk procedures solely because laboratory values are abnormal.
redFlags: Fever or systemic decline with ascites
counselling: Teach patients and families to seek care for new confusion, GI bleeding, fever, rapidly increasing abdominal distension or reduced urine output.
followUp: Decompensated cirrhosis requires coordinated hepatology follow-up, medication reconciliation, nutrition support and surveillance appropriate to the underlying liver disease.
examTrap: Ordering an ammonia level to decide whether confusion is hepatic encephalopathy while missing infection, bleeding or medication toxicity.
oneLinePearl: In cirrhosis, new ascites, bleeding, confusion or kidney injury means decompensation until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Hepatology Recommendations
Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver clinical resources

title: Hepatitis B and C: Test the Right Marker, Close the Loop
bottomLine: Viral hepatitis care starts with risk-based testing and correct interpretation. Hepatitis C antibody shows exposure and requires RNA testing to identify current infection; hepatitis B requires a serologic pattern rather than one isolated marker. Positive results need linkage to treatment, fibrosis assessment, vaccination and cancer-surveillance decisions when indicated.
recognize: Chronic HBV and HCV can be asymptomatic for years while progressive liver injury occurs.
People born in regions of higher HBV endemicity and people with blood, sexual or injection-related exposure risks may need targeted testing.
There is an effective hepatitis B vaccine, while no vaccine currently prevents hepatitis C.
differentiate: A positive anti-HCV result can represent current infection or past cleared infection; HCV RNA determines current viremia.
HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc answer different questions about current infection, immunity and prior exposure and must be interpreted together in context.
assessment: Ask country of birth and prior health care exposures where relevant, household or sexual exposure, injection or equipment sharing, transfusion history, tattoos or procedures, pregnancy, alcohol and other liver risks.
Use non-stigmatizing language and do not limit testing to patients who disclose injection drug use.
workup: Confirm current HCV infection with HCV RNA after a reactive antibody test.
Use current HBV serology and HBV DNA or liver staging as indicated; assess fibrosis and other causes of liver injury in chronic infection.
management: Link people with active HCV to direct-acting antiviral treatment because cure is achievable for most patients.

Use the 2025 CASL and AMMI Canada chronic hepatitis B guidance to determine monitoring versus antiviral therapy; treatment decisions depend on viral activity, liver injury, fibrosis or cirrhosis and other risk factors.
Vaccinate susceptible contacts and patients against hepatitis B and hepatitis A when indicated and follow public-health reporting requirements.
medicationSafety: Review drug interactions before HCV direct-acting antivirals.
HBV reactivation risk matters when patients receive significant immunosuppression or selected cancer therapies and should be screened or managed according to current guidance.
redFlags: Pregnancy with HBV requiring perinatal-prevention planning
counselling: Explain transmission prevention without unnecessary isolation and offer harm-reduction supports when relevant.
Successful HCV treatment does not create immunity; reinfection is possible after cure.
followUp: Confirm HCV treatment response with the recommended post-treatment viral assessment and continue cirrhosis-related surveillance when indicated.
Chronic HBV requires longitudinal monitoring even when immediate antiviral therapy is not indicated.
examTrap: Telling a patient that a positive hepatitis C antibody proves active chronic infection without ordering HCV RNA.
oneLinePearl: HCV antibody means exposure; RNA means current infection.
sourceBasis: CASL and AMMI Canada 2025 Chronic Hepatitis B Guideline
Public Health Agency of Canada Hepatitis B and C professional resources
Choosing Wisely Canada Hepatology Recommendations

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Flare or Complication?
bottomLine: In known or suspected IBD, do not label every increase in diarrhea as a flare. Exclude infection and look for obstruction, abscess, severe colitis, toxic megacolon, bleeding and medication complications before escalating immunosuppression.
recognize: Crohn disease can involve any GI segment and commonly causes abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, perianal disease or obstructive complications.
Ulcerative colitis causes continuous colonic mucosal inflammation beginning at the rectum and commonly presents with bloody diarrhea and urgency.
Extraintestinal manifestations can involve joints, skin, eyes and hepatobiliary disease.
differentiate: C. difficile and other enteric infection can mimic an IBD flare and can coexist with IBD.
IBS causes symptoms without the objective inflammatory, bleeding, weight-loss or structural complication pattern of active IBD.
assessment: Assess stool frequency and blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight, fever, hydration, abdominal distension, perianal symptoms, medication adherence and recent antibiotics or infections.
Review biologic or immunosuppressant use, vaccination status, pregnancy and thromboembolic risk.
workup: Use CBC, CRP and electrolytes plus stool testing for infection when an inflammatory flare is suspected; fecal calprotectin can help distinguish intestinal inflammation from functional symptoms in appropriate settings.
Endoscopy and cross-sectional imaging are used according to suspected location, severity and complication rather than reflexively at every symptom change.
management: Mild outpatient disease can be managed through an established gastroenterology plan, but severe bloody diarrhea, systemic toxicity, significant anemia, dehydration, obstruction or abscess concern requires urgent specialty or hospital care.
Do not escalate corticosteroids or biologics until major infectious mimics have been considered.
Long-term treatment aims for objective disease control and steroid-sparing remission rather than repeated steroid bursts.
medicationSafety: Immunosuppressive and biologic therapy requires infection screening, vaccine planning and agent-specific monitoring.
NSAIDs may worsen disease activity in some patients and should be used cautiously.
redFlags: Severe bloody diarrhea with systemic toxicity
counselling: Discuss medication adherence, smoking cessation in Crohn disease, nutrition and reproductive planning without recommending restrictive diets unsupported by evidence.
followUp: Coordinate objective disease monitoring, colon-cancer surveillance when indicated and specialist follow-up; persistent steroid dependence signals inadequate maintenance control.
examTrap: Giving another prednisone burst for worsening diarrhea without checking for C. difficile or a surgical complication.
oneLinePearl: Before calling it an IBD flare, rule out infection and complication.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Clinical Practice Guideline Library
Canadian IBD standards of care

title: Adrenal Insufficiency and Adrenal Crisis
bottomLine: Suspected adrenal crisis is a treat-before-proof emergency. Hypotension or shock, vomiting, abdominal symptoms, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia or hyperkalemia in a patient with known adrenal insufficiency or recent chronic glucocorticoid exposure should trigger immediate stress-dose glucocorticoid and fluid resuscitation while diagnostic testing proceeds.
recognize: Primary adrenal insufficiency can cause fatigue, weight loss, orthostasis, hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.
Secondary or glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency may lack hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia.
Infection, vomiting or diarrhea, surgery, trauma and abrupt interruption of chronic glucocorticoids can precipitate crisis.
differentiate: Adrenal crisis can mimic sepsis or gastroenteritis and can coexist with infection.
A random cortisol drawn during severe illness is not a reason to delay emergency glucocorticoid treatment when crisis is strongly suspected.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, glucose, volume status, fever or infection, vomiting or diarrhea, medication adherence and recent glucocorticoid exposure or taper.
Ask whether the patient has an emergency steroid plan, medical alert identification or injectable hydrocortisone.
workup: If feasible before steroids without delaying treatment, obtain cortisol and ACTH plus electrolytes, glucose and cause-directed testing.
Stable suspected chronic adrenal insufficiency requires formal endocrine evaluation and appropriate stimulation testing rather than empiric long-term steroids without diagnosis.
management: Give parenteral stress-dose hydrocortisone and isotonic fluid promptly in suspected crisis and correct hypoglycemia and electrolyte abnormalities in monitored acute care.
Treat the precipitating illness concurrently.
Known adrenal insufficiency requires sick-day dose escalation and emergency injection planning.
medicationSafety: Abrupt discontinuation after prolonged systemic glucocorticoid exposure can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.
Do not delay hydrocortisone in shock while waiting for confirmatory testing; short-term emergency treatment is safer than untreated crisis when suspicion is high.
redFlags: Persistent vomiting or diarrhea with known adrenal insufficiency
Recent chronic steroid exposure with acute collapse
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, emergency injectable glucocorticoid use and medical alert identification to patients with established adrenal insufficiency.
followUp: After stabilization, determine the type and cause of adrenal insufficiency, optimize chronic replacement and review prevention of future crises with endocrinology.
examTrap: Waiting for a cortisol result before giving hydrocortisone to a hypotensive vomiting patient with known Addison disease.
oneLinePearl: Adrenal crisis is one of the endocrine emergencies where treatment should beat confirmation.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism adrenal insufficiency emergency resources
BC Emergency Health Services Adrenal Crisis Guideline
Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guidelines when Canadian detail is unavailable

title: Acute Scrotal Pain: Torsion Until Excluded
bottomLine: Sudden severe unilateral testicular or lower-abdominal pain with nausea, a high-riding or abnormal-lie testis or absent cremasteric reflex is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. Surgical assessment must not be delayed for imaging when clinical suspicion is high.
recognize: Torsion often presents abruptly with severe unilateral scrotal pain, nausea or vomiting and can present as lower abdominal pain in adolescents.
The affected testis may be high-riding, horizontal or very tender, and the cremasteric reflex may be absent.
Epididymitis is generally more gradual and may include urinary or STI symptoms, but age and presentation overlap.
differentiate: Torsion of the appendix testis, epididymitis, hernia, trauma and tumour can cause scrotal pain, but none should delay torsion exclusion when the classic emergency pattern is present.
Urinalysis abnormalities do not safely exclude torsion.
assessment: Document exact onset, nausea or vomiting, trauma, urinary or STI symptoms and prior intermittent episodes.
Examine testicular lie, tenderness, swelling, cremasteric reflex and inguinal region while minimizing delay and distress.
workup: When suspicion is high, obtain immediate urologic or surgical consultation rather than waiting for Doppler ultrasound.
Ultrasound is appropriate when the diagnosis is uncertain and imaging can be obtained without delaying definitive care.
management: Arrange emergency surgical exploration and fixation when torsion is suspected.
Manual detorsion may be attempted by trained clinicians while awaiting surgery when appropriate, but apparent pain relief does not eliminate the need for operative management.
medicationSafety: Provide prompt analgesia and antiemetics; pain control does not interfere with the need for urgent diagnosis.
Do not give empiric STI antibiotics and discharge a patient with a high-suspicion torsion presentation.
counselling: Explain that testicular viability declines with time and why emergency surgery may be recommended before diagnostic certainty is absolute.
followUp: After torsion or orchiopexy, follow surgical guidance and address fertility or testicular health concerns as appropriate.
examTrap: Sending a classic torsion presentation for routine outpatient ultrasound before contacting urology or surgery.
oneLinePearl: Acute scrotum plus classic torsion findings is a clock, not an imaging project.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association Canadian Undergraduate Urology curriculum
Canadian urologic emergency standards

title: New Breast or Chest Mass: Diagnostic, Not Screening
bottomLine: A new palpable breast or chest mass is a diagnostic problem, not a routine screening problem. Characterize the mass and associated skin, nipple and nodal findings, choose age- and context-appropriate diagnostic imaging and make sure abnormal results proceed to tissue diagnosis or specialist assessment without being lost to follow-up.
recognize: Concerning features include a hard or fixed mass, skin dimpling or peau d'orange, spontaneous bloody nipple discharge, nipple retraction, persistent focal change or regional lymphadenopathy.
Many masses are benign, especially in younger patients, but clinical appearance alone cannot reliably exclude malignancy.
Pregnancy and lactation change the differential but do not make a persistent mass safe to ignore.
differentiate: Screening mammography is for asymptomatic eligible patients; a palpable mass needs diagnostic assessment even if the patient recently had a normal screening mammogram.
Mastitis generally produces pain, erythema and systemic or lactational context; persistent focal mass or nonresolving inflammation needs imaging and reassessment.
assessment: Ask duration and change, pain, relation to cycle, nipple discharge, skin changes, pregnancy or lactation, prior breast disease, family or genetic risk and hormone exposure.
Examine both breasts or chest, skin and nipples and relevant axillary or supraclavicular nodes.
workup: Use diagnostic breast imaging based on age, pregnancy or lactation and local pathway; ultrasound and diagnostic mammography are complementary in many adults.
Suspicious or discordant findings require biopsy or breast-specialist pathway rather than repeated observation.
management: Refer through the local breast diagnostic pathway when imaging or examination is suspicious.
Treat lactational mastitis supportively and with antibiotics when bacterial infection is clinically likely, but reassess a nonresolving focal abnormality for abscess or alternative diagnosis.
medicationSafety: Choose antibiotics compatible with lactation when treatment is needed and review allergies and local resistance patterns.
Do not repeatedly prescribe antibiotics for persistent inflammatory breast changes without reassessment.
redFlags: Persistent mass during pregnancy or lactation
counselling: Explain that most breast masses are not cancer while still emphasizing that persistence or suspicious features need definitive evaluation.
followUp: Track diagnostic imaging and biopsy results to completion; a normal screening history does not close the loop on a current palpable abnormality.
examTrap: Ordering a routine screening mammogram for a new palpable lump and treating the screening result as the diagnostic endpoint.
oneLinePearl: A symptom changes the pathway: new lump equals diagnostic assessment.
sourceBasis: Ontario Health Cancer Care Ontario Breast Cancer Screening and Diagnosis Pathway Map
Provincial breast diagnostic pathways

title: Menopause: Treat Symptoms, Not Hormone Levels
bottomLine: Typical perimenopause and menopause are clinical diagnoses; routine hormone testing is usually unnecessary in the expected age range. Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for bothersome vasomotor symptoms in appropriate patients, but route and regimen must match uterine status, contraindications, risk profile and patient preference.
recognize: Cycle change, hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbance and genitourinary symptoms are common during the menopause transition.
Genitourinary syndrome can cause vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency and recurrent urinary symptoms and may persist without treatment.
Abnormal bleeding, especially postmenopausal bleeding, is not a routine menopause symptom and requires evaluation.
differentiate: Thyroid disease, pregnancy, medication effects, sleep disorders and mood disorders can mimic or amplify menopause symptoms.
FSH testing is not routinely needed to diagnose typical menopause in the expected age range; premature ovarian insufficiency or atypical presentations require a different evaluation.
assessment: Ask the most bothersome symptoms, menstrual pattern, uterus status, pregnancy or contraception needs, VTE and cardiovascular history, breast or estrogen-dependent cancer history, liver disease and patient treatment preferences.
Assess bone, cardiovascular, sexual, sleep and mental-health concerns based on the individual rather than attributing every symptom to menopause.
workup: Do not order broad sex-hormone panels for routine diagnosis of typical menopause.
Investigate abnormal uterine bleeding, suspected premature ovarian insufficiency or alternative diagnoses with the appropriate pathway.
management: Ontario Health's menopause quality standard identifies menopausal hormone therapy as first-line treatment for vasomotor symptoms after assessment of risks, benefits, contraindications and individual needs.
Systemic estrogen requires endometrial protection with an appropriate progestogen or equivalent strategy when the uterus is present.
Use evidence-based nonhormonal options when MHT is contraindicated or not desired and use local vaginal therapy for genitourinary symptoms when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not use unregulated compounded 'bioidentical' hormone products as a safer substitute for Health Canada-approved therapy.

Known or suspected breast or estrogen-dependent cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, active liver disease and important thrombotic or cardiovascular histories require individualized assessment before systemic MHT.
redFlags: Severe unexplained headache or neurologic symptoms
counselling: Discuss expected benefits, route-specific risks and alternatives using shared decision-making rather than presenting hormone therapy as universally dangerous or universally necessary.
followUp: Review symptom benefit, bleeding pattern, adverse effects and evolving health risks after treatment initiation or change; continue preventive care appropriate to age and risk.
examTrap: Ordering serial FSH and estradiol levels to prove typical menopause or prescribing estrogen alone to a patient with an intact uterus.
oneLinePearl: Typical menopause is clinical; treatment is symptom- and risk-driven.
sourceBasis: Ontario Health Menopause Quality Standard 2025
Canadian Menopause Society Menopause Hub and SOGC/CMS Guideline 422 series
